chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Muthanna al-Hannat, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed li'an with his wife and denied her child, then admitted his own lie after the li'an and claimed that her child was his child. [I asked:] Will she be returned to him? He (peace be upon him) said: No, and it is not [merely] an honour; she will not be returned to him, nor will she be permissible to him until the Day of Resurrection.

He (the narrator) said: And I asked him, 'Who inherits the child?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'His mother.' So I said, 'What is your view if the mother dies and the boy inherits her, then the boy dies afterwards, who would inherit him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'His maternal uncles.' So I said, 'If the father acknowledges him, does the father inherit?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, but the father does not inherit from the son.'
ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance and marital status rulings for a child of li'an if the father admits the child is his?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the permanent marital bond (la'nan) resulting from li'an, emphasizing that the wife remains forbidden to the husband even if he later admits the child is his, a ruling rooted in the finality of the cursing procedure. It further delineates inheritance dynamics, establishing that while the father inherits from the son, the son does not inherit from the father, highlighting the distinct legal status of the child in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the principle that li'an severs the reciprocal inheritance link, a nuance critical for understanding family law in the Imami tradition.
